A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same redundancy-based adversarial attack framework. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 has no appendix; v2 adds Appendix A, which was included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet attack experiments, including component sensitivity studies and the comparisons in Tables 1 and 2.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds comparator results, PiT/Swin surrogate results, VLLM evaluations and clean-accuracy redundancy tests in Appendix A.

M1.justification: The five attack components and online policy remain. Section 3.3 changes robustification-token initialization from zero to random. v2 also specifies PiT edge-padding and Swin attention-layer token insertion, although v1 had already mentioned these architectures without explaining their implementations.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K classification remains the data and task foundation. v2 adds an image-plus-candidate-label prompting scenario for VLLMs and partial-observation tests using dropped input tokens in Appendix A. These extend test conditions without adding a dataset or a different application domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds the ViT-specific attacks TGR, GNS and FPR to the retained ViT-B/16 comparison, substantially strengthening the comparator coverage. They also participate in the PiT-B and VLLM comparisons; the Swin-T comparison explicitly excludes them because implementations are unavailable.

E3.justification: v2 introduces VLLM testing with 1,000 candidate labels and Appendix A protocols measuring clean top-1 accuracy under token, attention-weight, head and neuron dropping. Section 3.2 also replaces its stated seven-model roster with eight models matching the retained plots. The original 1,000-image sample size, 16/255 perturbation budget and ten attack steps remain; rerunning retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: New Appendix A and Figure 7 directly test the redundancy premise through four clean-accuracy sensitivity studies on ViT and PiT. These differ from the existing attack-success analyses. The original attention sparsity, head shuffling, clean-token, ghost-MoE and robust-token studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. Averages across target models do not constitute repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original Table 2 rows remain unchanged, including the method's 86.9% ViT average. v2 adds substantial results for new comparators, PiT/Swin surrogates, VLLMs and redundancy tests. For example, newly reported ResNet-50 attack success is 86.0% from PiT-B and 85.2% from Swin-T. Descriptions of retained curves are also corrected, including the clean-token deterioration threshold changing from above 0.6 to above 0.4.

T1.justification: Section 4 adds an explicit expected-loss objective and evaluates the categorical-policy log-probability derivative within the existing policy-gradient formulation. The minimax objectives remain unchanged. No theorem, proof or transferability bound accompanies the new introductory claim about improving a theoretical bound.

C1.justification: The central claim that computational redundancy improves adversarial transferability remains. v2 explicitly extends the abstract's generality claim to VLLMs and adds a contribution claim about improving a theoretical transferability bound. Highlighting online policy learning as a separate contribution promotes a component already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds a shared-information explanation for head-shuffling transferability and discusses architectural constraints on robust-token placement. Appendix A introduces concrete claims about accuracy preservation under substantial dropping. These qualifications are not uniformly supported: Figure 7 shows ViT head-drop accuracy below 10% at 50% dropping, despite the accompanying high-accuracy claim.

D1.justification: v2 documents integration of policy learning into MI-FGSM, PiT padding, Swin token insertion, exact VLLM variants and candidate-label inputs. Reproducibility remains incomplete, and the new PiT/Swin descriptions call token optimization gradient ascent despite Equation 8 minimizing over those tokens.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against ViT-specific attacks and research on token reduction, redundant attention heads and MoE. It explicitly distinguishes its elementwise attention manipulation from FPR's attention-block dropping, attributes clean-feature inspiration, and adds a dedicated redundancy-related-work discussion in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, related work is condensed, and the policy-learning subsection is rewritten and promoted to Section 4. Experiments gain surrogate-specific headings. The central narrative and much of the operation-by-operation exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview diagram, a VLLM comparison chart and a four-panel appendix figure. Table 2 becomes a three-surrogate comparison. The four retained analysis plots are enlarged and redrawn with clearer legends and MI-FGSM reference lines; their underlying curves remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added ViT-specific comparisons, explicit PiT/Swin results and clearer method presentation address important gaps in v1. However, expanded Table 2 mixes averages that include and exclude the surrogate target, Appendix A's accuracy-preservation claims conflict with Figure 7, and the new theoretical-bound claim lacks a bound. These material gains coexist with new reporting and interpretation problems, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
